ANSWER OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. TO  
MOTION FOR EXPEDITED ACTION OF CONSTELLATION  
ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
 
 
Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.213, PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) submits this answer to Constellation Energy Generation, 
LLC’s (“Constellation”) November 21, 2025, Motion for Expedited Action (“Motion”).1   
 
The Motion recognizes that the subject matter of the captioned proceedings 
overlaps the issues in the recently-initiated, industry-wide ANOPR2 proceeding.3  The 
Motion nonetheless seeks a “full order on the merits” applicable solely in the PJM Region, 
“even while the Commission develops a comprehensive rule in response to the ANOPR” 
 
1  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Expedited Action of Constellation Energy 
Generation, LLC, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (Nov. 21, 2025).   
2  
Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, Advance Notice 
of Proposed Rulemaking, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025) (“ANOPR”).   
3  
Motion at 4 (noting that “the interconnection of large loads to the transmission 
system” is “the subject of both the ANOPR and this show cause proceeding”).

2 
applicable nationwide.4  The Motion seeks relief prior to any Commission determinations 
prompted by the ANOPR on foundational issues, including jurisdictional boundaries.  The 
Motion invites the Commission to run afoul of the principle that agencies should defer 
taking action in specific adjudicatory matters where such action would supplant ongoing 
generic rulemakings.5  The Commission should not take the bait.   
If that was not enough, PJM has been engaged with its stakeholders—including 
Constellation—in a Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) process to assist PJM’s Board of 
Managers in determining how to address this important, yet extremely complex, issue.  The 
ANOPR clearly states that it was “not intended in any way to discourage public utilities 
from making filings to address these and similar issues under FPA section 205.”6 
 
By seeking an expedited order on the merits in these proceedings, the Motion 
requests relief that not only pre-empts the ANOPR docket but also the CIFP process and 
any section 205 filings the ANOPR goes out of its way to avoid discouraging.  The Motion 
attempts to lock in its movant’s desired outcome while foreclosing possible solutions under 
consideration by PJM’s Board of Mangers as developed in the expedited CIFP process.  
PJM encourages clear Commission guidance on these important issues, but not in the 
Motion’s requested fashion.    
 
4  
Motion at 4.   
5  
See City of Anaheim v. FERC, 723 F.2d 656, 659 (9th Cir. 1984) (“[A]gencies may 
not use adjudication to circumvent the Administrative Procedure Act’s rulemaking 
procedures” and adjudication should not “supplant a pending rule-making 
proceeding.”); Duke Energy Moss Landing LLC, 86 FERC ¶ 61,227, at 61,815–16 
(1999) (implying that an adjudication would circumvent the Administrative 
Procedure Act’s rulemaking provisions if it supplants a pending rulemaking). 
6  
ANOPR at P 32.

3 
 
Should the Commission feel inclined to address the issues raised by Constellation 
in its Motion through action on the Section 206 filing, the Commission should be cognizant 
that a set of rules or guidelines that are applicable only to the PJM market will not create a 
rational, durable, and predictable pathway for the national issues associated with large load 
interconnection. A “PJM-only” solution will only encourage data centers to shop for 
locations based not on the underlying values of a particular site but instead on exploiting 
regulatory arbitrage created by inconsistent regulatory treatment across regions.  Such an 
approach is not consistent with the President’s Executive Order which focuses on the need 
for development of AI infrastructure as a national, not regional, imperative.  
ANSWER 
 
PJM’s CIFP process concerning the integration of large loads has been ongoing 
since September, culminating in presentations before PJM’s Board of Managers on 
November 19, 2025.  Various stakeholders or stakeholder groups presented a total of twelve 
proposal packages to the Board. Among those groups were the “Joint Stakeholders,” a 
group including Constellation (Constellation included the Joint Stakeholders’ package as 
an exhibit to its comments on the ANOPR).7  The Board is now considering the 
stakeholders’ various proposals and will soon determine and announce how it plans to 
proceed.   
 
In addition, initial comments in the ANOPR process initiated by the Commission 
at the request of the Secretary of Energy were filed on November 21, 2025.  As 
Constellation acknowledges, the ANOPR process involves issues identical to those at issue 
 
7  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Supporting Comments of Constellation Energy 
Generation, LLC, Docket No. RM26-4-000, Exhibit 1 (Nov. 21, 2025) 
(“Constellation Comments”).

4 
in these dockets.  The Secretary of Energy has directed the Commission to take “final 
action” on the ANOPR by April 30, 2026.   
 
Rather than await the results of the ANOPR processes, without regard for City of 
Anaheim v. FERC, and indifferent to the ongoing deliberative CIFP process, the Motion 
asks the Commission to make a merits decision that would implement its movant’s 
preferred outcomes in these consolidated dockets immediately.  The Motion’s requested 
relief includes a proposed finding that PJM’s Tariff is unjust and unreasonable and an 
accompanying order establishing a “full replacement rate.”8  While the components of the 
replacement rate are not specified in the Motion, the Constellation Comments in the 
ANOPR proceedings request the Commission to adopt certain options that PJM proposed 
in its Answer to the Commission’s order to show cause in these dockets.9  Specifically, the 
movant seeks adoption of PJM options 2,10 4,11 5,12 and 713 “as clarified and modified by 
 
8  
Motion at 1.   
9  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket 
Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Show Cause Answer”).   
10  
Option 2, as conceived by PJM, already exists in its Tariff.  It involves co-located 
load and generation at the same point of interconnection, but separately metered.  
The load would take Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”).  PJM 
Show Cause Answer, Exhibit A.   
11  
Option 4 involves co-located load behind generation with protection systems to 
prevent delivery of energy from the grid to the load in the event the generation goes 
offline.  This was essentially the fully-isolated co-located load configuration that 
motivated Constellation’s complaint.  PJM Show Cause Answer, Exhibit A.   
12  
Option 5 is similar to Option 4, with an allowance for back-up service from the 
PJM system with permission.  PJM Show Cause Answer, Exhibit A.   
13  
Option 7 involves co-located load and generation where the load is willing to curtail 
in advance of Emergency Procedures.  PJM Show Cause Answer, Exhibit A.

5 
Constellation.”14  The movant also asks the Commission to reject PJM option 6,15 find that 
it lacks jurisdiction “over behind-the-meter sales between a co-located generator and load,” 
require Transmission Owners to “provide timely participation in relevant studies requested 
by PJM and in the interconnection agreement process,” and require Transmission Owners 
“to process load interconnection requests on the same timelines regardless of 
configuration.”16   
 
If the Commission does not immediately prescribe this preferred “full replacement 
rate,” the Motion seeks alternative “targeted” relief including: (1) clarification of 
“jurisdictional boundaries consistent with the ANOPR,” (2) rejection of “a one-size-fits-all 
firm transmission regime based on gross rates,” and (3) requiring Transmission Owners to 
cooperate in processing large load co-location studies.17   
 
As PJM previously explained in the captioned proceedings, it believes its Tariff 
remains just and reasonable.18  Based on Commission guidance, PJM is willing to 
implement improvements or clarifications to further facilitate large load interconnections.  
PJM also recognizes that the issues presented by integrating large data center loads into the 
interstate transmission system are complex and, thus far, have eluded Commission 
 
14  
Constellation Comments at 45.   
15  
Option 6 involves a large load connecting as a network customer and bringing its 
own generation.  PJM Show Cause Answer, Exhibit A.   
16  
Constellation Comments at 45-46.   
17  
Motion at 2.  Constellation embellishes these requests in the Constellation 
Comments at 47-51.   
18  
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Answer and 
Motion to Dismiss of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-20-000, 
at 12-16 (Dec. 12, 2024); PJM Show Cause Answer at 4 (“The record will support 
a finding that PJM’s existing Tariff remains just and reasonable.”).

6 
guidance and stakeholder consensus and are now the subject of a nationwide rulemaking.  
PJM appreciates Constellation’s participation in the CIFP process and other proceedings at 
FERC.  But participation alone should not translate into pre-emption of orderly regulatory 
processes and collaborative, industry-wide efforts to inform the PJM Board of Managers’ 
action.  After all, the Secretary of Energy sought a national rulemaking from the 
Commission, not a solution only applicable to one particular region. 
The Commission should complete its ANOPR process by the April 30, 2026, date 
the Secretary of Energy has directed, and allow PJM’s CIFP process to reach a conclusion 
without foreclosing any options available to PJM’s Board.   
CONCLUSION 
 
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should deny the Motion.   
Respectfully submitted,
